summary.overview: Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble structural proteins built from one repeating type of secondary structure. α-Keratin (coiled α-helices, many disulfides) gives hair and horn their strength; collagen (a Gly–X–Y triple helix) gives tendons their tensile strength; silk fibroin (stacked β-sheets) is strong and flexible but does not stretch.

sections.heading: General features
points: Long strands or sheets made of simple repeating secondary-structure elements, which give strength and/or flexibility.
Insoluble in water: hydrophobic residues inside AND on the surface are buried when many chains pack into supramolecular complexes.

sections.heading: α-Keratin
points: Found in mammals: hair, wool, nails, horn, hooves and the outer skin; part of the intermediate-filament family.
Two right-handed α-helices wind around each other into a left-handed coiled coil, like a rope.
The helix–helix contact surface is hydrophobic (Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Met, Phe).
Disulfide cross-links add strength. The hardest keratin, rhinoceros horn, has about 18% Cys.
Permanent waving: reduce the disulfides, set the hair in curls, then re-oxidise to form new disulfides in the new positions.

sections.heading: Collagen
points: Gives strength to tendons, cartilage, bone matrix and cornea; tensile strength is greater than steel wire of the same cross-section.
Each chain is a left-handed helix with about 3 residues per turn (not an α-helix). Three chains supertwist into a right-handed triple helix.
The repeating sequence is Gly–X–Y, where X is often Pro and Y often 4-hydroxyproline (4-Hyp). The chain is about 35% Gly, 11% Ala and 21% Pro + Hyp.
Gly must sit at every third position because only its tiny side chain fits in the crowded centre of the triple helix.
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need vitamin C. Without it, under-hydroxylated collagen is unstable, causing scurvy in humans, guinea pigs, other primates and fruit bats.
Covalent cross-links between Lys, hydroxylysine and His residues increase with age, making connective tissue stiffer and more brittle.
Gelatin is denatured collagen; it is poor in essential amino acids, so it has little nutritional value.

sections.heading: Silk fibroin
points: Made by insects and spiders. It consists of antiparallel β-sheets rich in Ala and Gly, whose small side chains let the sheets pack closely and interlock.
Stabilised by H-bonds and van der Waals contacts, with no covalent cross-links, which makes it flexible.
It does not stretch, because the β-strands are already almost fully extended.

keyTerms.definition: Elongated, insoluble structural protein built from a repeating secondary structure.
Two α-helices twisted around each other, as in α-keratin.
Three left-handed collagen chains supertwisted in a right-handed sense.
Collagen's sequence motif: Gly every third residue, X often Pro, Y often 4-Hyp.
Post-translationally hydroxylated Pro that stabilises collagen (needs vitamin C).
Vitamin C deficiency causing defective collagen, fragile capillaries and bleeding.
β-Sheet protein rich in Ala and Gly; strong, flexible and non-stretchy.

examTips: Keratin = α-helix coiled coil + disulfides; collagen = triple helix with Gly every 3rd residue; silk = β-sheet.
Collagen chains are LEFT-handed helices with a RIGHT-handed supertwist; keratin is the opposite (right-handed helices, left-handed supertwist).
Vitamin C is needed to hydroxylate Pro and Lys in collagen, not to make the chains.
Wool stretches (helices extend); silk doesn't (sheets are already extended).

questions.stem: Why are fibrous proteins such as keratin and collagen insoluble in water?

options.text: They are rich in hydrophobic residues, inside and on the surface, buried by packing many chains together
options.why: Close packing hides the hydrophobic surfaces from water, producing insoluble fibres.

options.text: They contain no amino acids, only long lipid chains, which repel water like the tails of a membrane
options.why: They are proteins made of amino acids.

options.text: They are made mostly of charged residues, which bind each other so tightly that water can't get in
options.why: Highly charged proteins tend to be soluble.

options.text: They are permanently denatured, so their unfolded chains clump together as soon as they are made
options.why: They are functional, folded proteins.

questions.stem: Which description of α-keratin structure is correct?

options.text: Two right-handed α-helices wound into a left-handed coiled coil, joined by a hydrophobic surface
options.why: Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Met and Phe line the interface, and disulfides cross-link neighbouring chains.

options.text: Three left-handed helices wound into a right-handed triple helix, with Gly at every third residue
options.why: That describes collagen.

options.text: Stacked antiparallel β-sheets rich in Ala and Gly, whose small side chains interlock tightly
options.why: That describes silk fibroin.

options.text: A single compact globular domain with a hydrophobic core and a polar surface
options.why: Keratin is fibrous.

questions.stem: Rhinoceros horn is one of the hardest α-keratins, with about 18% of its residues being cysteine. Why does this make it so hard?

options.text: Many cysteines form covalent disulfide cross-links between keratin chains
options.why: More disulfide 'staples' make the fibre stiffer and harder.

options.text: Cysteine makes the keratin helices left-handed, which packs them more tightly
options.why: Handedness comes from L-amino acid geometry, not Cys content.

options.text: Cysteine is the most hydrophobic amino acid, so it excludes water from the horn
options.why: Cys's key role here is covalent disulfide formation.

options.text: Cysteine forms extra peptide bonds between chains, joining them into one polymer
options.why: Cross-links between chains are disulfide, not peptide, bonds.

questions.stem: How does a 'permanent wave' treatment curl hair?

options.text: A reducing agent breaks disulfides, the hair is set in curlers, then an oxidant forms new disulfides
options.why: Moving the covalent cross-links fixes the new shape.

options.text: Heat breaks the peptide bonds in keratin and then re-forms them in new positions around the curler
options.why: Peptide bonds are not broken.

options.text: Water dissolves the keratin, which then re-crystallises in a curled shape as the hair slowly dries
options.why: Keratin is insoluble in water.

options.text: Collagen is added to the hair shaft, where it forms a triple helix that holds the curl in place
options.why: Hair is keratin; collagen plays no role.

questions.stem: Why must glycine occupy every third position in the collagen sequence (Gly–X–Y)?

options.text: Its tiny side chain (H) is the only one that fits in the crowded centre of the triple helix
options.why: Any larger residue at these positions distorts the triple helix.

options.text: Glycine forms disulfide bonds between the three chains, which holds the triple helix together
options.why: Glycine has no –SH group.

options.text: Glycine is hydroxylated by a vitamin C-dependent enzyme, which lets it H-bond to the other chains
options.why: Pro and Lys are hydroxylated, not Gly.

options.text: Glycine is the only chiral amino acid, so it alone gives the collagen chain its left-handed twist
options.why: Glycine is the only achiral standard amino acid.

questions.stem: How are collagen chains arranged in the triple helix?

options.text: Each chain is a left-handed helix (about 3 residues per turn); the three supertwist right-handedly
options.why: The opposite twisting of chain and supertwist gives great tensile strength.

options.text: Each chain is a right-handed α-helix, and two of the chains wind into a left-handed coiled coil
options.why: That describes α-keratin.

options.text: The three chains lie side by side as flat parallel β-sheets, held together by backbone H-bonds
options.why: That is closer to silk fibroin.

options.text: A single chain folds back on itself into a compact globular domain with a hydrophobic core
options.why: Collagen is a three-chain fibrous protein.

questions.stem: A guinea pig fed only cereal pellets with no added vitamin C develops bleeding gums, a rough coat and painful joints. What is the biochemical defect?

options.text: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases lack their vitamin C cofactor, so collagen's triple helix is unstable
options.why: Guinea pigs, like humans, cannot make ascorbate; without 4-Hyp collagen is weak, so capillaries are fragile (scurvy).

options.text: The collagen genes are deleted in guinea pigs, so no collagen is made unless vitamin C switches them on
options.why: The collagen genes are normal; the problem is post-translational modification.

options.text: Glycine cannot be synthesised without vitamin C, so every third residue of collagen is missing
options.why: Glycine is non-essential and is not the issue.

options.text: Disulfide bonds in keratin are reduced without vitamin C, so the skin and coat lose their strength
options.why: The connective-tissue defect lies in collagen.

questions.stem: A mutation replaces a single glycine in a Gly–X–Y repeat of type I collagen with a bulky residue, causing fragile bones. Why does one substitution have such a large effect?

options.text: The bulky side chain can't fit in the helix centre, so it disrupts packing of all three chains
options.why: This is the molecular basis of osteogenesis imperfecta-type defects.

options.text: Glycine is needed for hydroxylation by vitamin C, so the whole chain is left under-hydroxylated
options.why: Hydroxylation targets Pro and Lys.

options.text: The mutation changes collagen into a keratin-like protein, which cannot form bone matrix fibres
options.why: A point mutation does not change protein identity.

options.text: Collagen does not need a regular sequence, so the mutation must have deleted the whole chain
options.why: The strict Gly–X–Y repeat is essential.

questions.stem: Why do tendons and skin become stiffer and more brittle in older animals?

options.text: Covalent cross-links between Lys, hydroxylysine and His in collagen accumulate with age
options.why: More cross-links reduce flexibility.

options.text: Collagen is gradually replaced by silk fibroin, which is stiffer and much less elastic
options.why: Mammals don't make fibroin.

options.text: Glycine is slowly removed from collagen, so the chains can no longer slide
options.why: The sequence doesn't change with age.

options.text: Vitamin C levels rise with age, so collagen becomes over-hydroxylated and rigid
options.why: The change is in cross-linking.

questions.stem: β-Aminopropionitrile, found in some Lathyrus (sweet pea) seeds, inhibits lysyl oxidase, the enzyme that starts collagen cross-linking. What would you expect in animals eating these seeds?

options.text: Weak connective tissue (bone deformities, weak blood vessels), as collagen can't be cross-linked
options.why: Triple helices still form, but without cross-links the fibres lack tensile strength (lathyrism).

options.text: Excessively rigid tendons and joints, because collagen fibres become over-cross-linked
options.why: Blocking cross-linking makes tissue weaker, not stiffer.

options.text: Harder hooves and horns, because more keratin disulfides form when lysyl oxidase is blocked
options.why: Lysyl oxidase acts on collagen and elastin, not keratin disulfides.

options.text: No visible effect, because collagen fibres are strong enough without any covalent cross-links
options.why: Cross-links are essential for collagen strength.

questions.stem: Gelatin, made from collagen, is a poor protein source in an animal's diet. Why?

options.text: Its composition is dominated by Gly, Pro and Hyp and is low in several essential amino acids
options.why: Protein quality depends on supplying every essential amino acid.

options.text: It cannot be digested by any protease in the gut, so it passes through the intestine unchanged
options.why: Gelatin is denatured collagen and is easily digested.

options.text: It contains mainly D-amino acids, which animals cannot use to build their own proteins
options.why: Its amino acids are L-isomers.

options.text: It is a carbohydrate, not a protein, so it supplies energy but no amino acids
options.why: Gelatin is a protein.

questions.stem: What allows the β-sheets of silk fibroin to pack so closely?

options.text: Fibroin is rich in Ala and Gly, whose small side chains interlock between stacked sheets
options.why: Small R groups allow tight packing, stabilised by H-bonds and van der Waals contacts.

options.text: It contains many disulfide cross-links, which pull the sheets tightly against each other
options.why: Fibroin has essentially no covalent cross-links, which is why it is flexible.

options.text: It is rich in bulky Trp and Tyr residues, whose rings stack flat between neighbouring sheets
options.why: Bulky residues would prevent close packing.

options.text: It forms α-helical coiled coils, which pack more closely than any other secondary structure
options.why: That is keratin; fibroin is β-sheet.

questions.stem: Wool can be stretched to nearly twice its length when steamed, but silk barely stretches. What is the structural explanation?

options.text: Wool's α-helices can be pulled into extended chains; silk's β-strands are already almost fully extended
options.why: Secondary structure determines mechanical behaviour.

options.text: Silk contains more disulfide bonds than wool, and these covalent cross-links stop its chains from sliding
options.why: Wool keratin is the disulfide-rich one.

options.text: Wool is made of collagen, whose triple helix unwinds in steam and lets the fibre stretch to twice its length
options.why: Wool is α-keratin.

options.text: Silk is a globular protein whose compact folded domains cannot be pulled apart without breaking the fibre
options.why: Silk fibroin is fibrous.

questions.stem: Silk is strong yet very flexible. Which feature explains its flexibility?

options.text: Its sheets are held only by weak non-covalent interactions, with no covalent cross-links
options.why: Sheets can slide slightly relative to each other without breaking.

options.text: It is a coiled coil of α-helices that can stretch and spring back like a telephone cord
options.why: That is keratin.

options.text: It contains 18% cysteine, whose disulfide bonds can break and re-form as the fibre bends
options.why: That is rhinoceros-horn keratin.

options.text: It is a triple helix whose three chains can slide past each other when the fibre is bent
options.why: That is collagen.

flashcards.back: Long strands or sheets of one repeating secondary structure; strength or flexibility; insoluble (hydrophobic surfaces buried by packing).
Two right-handed α-helices in a left-handed coiled coil; hydrophobic interface; disulfide cross-links. Hair, wool, nails, horn.

flashcards.front: How does a permanent wave work?
flashcards.back: Reduce the disulfides → set the curl → re-oxidise to form new disulfides.
Gly–X–Y (X often Pro, Y often 4-Hyp). About 35% Gly, 11% Ala, 21% Pro + Hyp.
Each chain is a left-handed helix (~3 residues per turn); three chains form a right-handed supertwist (triple helix).
Only Gly is small enough to fit in the crowded centre of the triple helix.
Vitamin C is the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases. Deficiency → unstable collagen → scurvy (humans, primates, guinea pigs, fruit bats).

flashcards.front: Why does connective tissue stiffen with age?
flashcards.back: Covalent Lys, hydroxylysine and His cross-links accumulate in collagen.
Antiparallel β-sheets rich in Ala and Gly, packed closely; H-bonds and van der Waals; no covalent cross-links.

flashcards.front: Why is silk flexible but not stretchy?
flashcards.back: Flexible: only weak interactions between sheets. Not stretchy: the β-strands are already fully extended.
